summary:
Mayotte is a French overseas department in the Indian Ocean and stands under the French national framework, including its places of deprivation of liberty.

Trans detainees in Mayotte's establishments are held according to the gender shown on their identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them; placement follows the document marker rather than anatomy.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. The opinion extends to Mayotte's local jails as French establishments.

Legal gender change without surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatric certificates or proof of medical intervention was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017; a court appearance is still required to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be done at the registry office. The National Assembly also voted the simplification of legal gender change. French law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity: article 225-1 of the Penal Code was amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that account. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023, after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the written law is not the whole of what a couple faces. Same-sex marriage has been legal here since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law, as available.

A 16 May 2020 French report recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared with around 1,380 in 2018; the figure is national and covers homophobic and transphobic incidents together, not Mayotte alone.

Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the government, with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.
tangentialFactors:
The 16 May 2020 French report recording a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019 is a national figure covering homophobic and transphobic incidents together; it is not specific to Mayotte and does not by itself indicate the island's own incident rate.

France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, though transgender rights organisations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery performed in-country was legalised in 1979 after previously only being accessible abroad.

The National Academy of Medicine has characterised increased demand for gender care as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution, without changing actual practice.

Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces. Conversion therapy was banned by Senate vote 7 December 2020, National Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022, with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine.

In March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms.

Article 225-1 of the Penal Code, as amended on 18 November 2016, and the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, recruitment, internships and training. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and hate-crime provisions cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination.

Transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, with a recommendation for informed consent and self-determination.

Legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the government, with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.

A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law, as available.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Mayotte-specific incident data on violence against trans people; the 36% rise figure from the 16 May 2020 report is national and combines homophobic and transphobic incidents, so no island-level prevalence can be stated.

No Mayotte-specific enforcement record for the anti-discrimination provisions or the transphobia aggravating factor is documented in this inventory; how these national rules are applied on the island is unresolved.

The status of the under-18 medical transition ban legislation is unresolved beyond 23 July 2024, with no update recorded in the sources.

No region-specific data on detention conditions in Mayotte's own establishments is documented; the CGLPL findings cited are based on inspections at mainland French facilities, extended to Mayotte only by virtue of French law applying.
